text:
Chosen option: Self-contained by default, linked on a server.

Smaller served pages; two output modes to build and test.

RichView is built first for analysts, above all data analysts in every industry, who publish internal or external analysis and do that work with a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. The agent writes and revises the source; the analyst directs, reviews the rendered story and owns its claims. Every authoring capability works for an agent without a GUI. RichView is not built for zero-code business users, newsrooms or teams that need roles and approvals; those audiences belong to sibling products only if INT-33 to INT-35 accept them.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26 ("the primary audience are analysts, even more data analysts, across all industries, publishing internal or external focused analysis"); recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text: Truthfulness of the evidence is not something RichView maximizes; RichView maximizes other targets. What RichView guarantees is that a story stays traceable and editable: every chart and figure can show where its data came from, and the author can inspect and change every presentation choice. Presentation choices that trade literal precision for readability, such as smoothed curves on a line chart, are the author's to make and are not ruled out for fidelity.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: smooth line curves hide whether the data was that smooth, so fidelity is not a key value; it should be traceable and editable, but RichView maximizes other things. Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text: RichView presents analysis. By default it reads data the agent or the author's pipeline has exported into the report folder. Live connections to data sources are in scope as a secondary path: they belong to RichView Publish, so a CMS-style publishing setup can serve stories from live data. Connectors come from an existing third-party engine that already offers a set of connectors, so RichView does not build them from scratch. Exported data stays the default for every report.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: live connectors are definitely part of RichView; exported data is the default; live connections are secondary, part of RichView Publishing through a CMS setup, ideally using a third-party engine with existing connectors. Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text: RichView is a tool the author's agent calls. People bring their own agent; RichView has no chat interface, makes no LLM or speech-to-text calls, stores no model keys (no BYOK), runs no agent loop and does not generate slides or decks from prompts. The author's own agent does all language work. The main way to work is local: the author's agent uses RichView through its CLI and MCP server. A RichView server may at most expose MCP to an agent; it never adds a chat interface. Voice and chat front ends are sibling demos, never core (INT-34).
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "People bring in the agent, and we will not have any chat interface. At max, if people will be using something like the server, it can work as a MCP on top of the agent itself. But the main way to work with this is locally, having an agent: MCP and CLI." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text:
RichView is built first for analysts, above all data analysts in every industry, who publish internal or external analysis and do that work with a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. The agent writes and revises the source; the analyst directs, reviews the rendered story and owns its claims. Every authoring capability works for an agent without a GUI. Most of RichView's communication targets analysts.

Writers in general can use it too: analysts and journalists, someone hosting their own small RichView server as a personal site or blog, and later a newsroom. Roles and approvals belong to RichView's servers, never to the core: RichView Publish (external-facing) and an internal-facing server (working name RichView Cowork, sharing much of Publish's core) both have a basic set of roles, such as reader, author, owner, and who may edit, delete and share. RichView is not built for zero-code business users.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26. First: "the primary audience are analysts, even more data analysts, across all industries, publishing internal or external focused analysis". Then, on whether Publish is an exception: writers in general can be users, analysts and journalists; people may host their own RichView server as a personal page or blog, or a newsroom later; target most communication at analysts; Publish can have roles and approvals while the core stays without them; the internal-facing server, maybe called RichView Cowork, also needs basic roles (reader, owner, who can edit, delete, share), so roles are part of RichView. Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request; this replaces the agent-recorded edit of 11:29.

text:
RichView has no WYSIWYG or full browser editor, and never will: people should see and touch what is underneath, the Rich Markdown source. Real authoring happens in the author's editor (VS Code with live preview, or possibly a RichView desktop app later) and through their agent, with Git as the history. The browser playground stays: a source pane with live preview for trying the format and styles, with loading, copying and downloading, and no accounts.

On a RichView server (Publish, Cowork), the browser offers only actions where they make sense:
- approving what gets published: open the pending change online and click yes or no;
- quick source edits by the page's author: when signed in as its author, Edit opens the page's Rich Markdown source in an embedded VS Code-style editor with syntax highlighting, and the server checks that the edited report still validates and renders before it is saved.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "Avoid. I definitely want to avoid a full browser editor. If we would go with something, we will use VS Code, or have our own desktop app. The online editor can have only features where it makes sense, for example accepting something before it is published: you open it online and click yes or no. It will never be a full WYSIWYG. The only thing I want is that when you publish a page, want to edit it and are logged in as the author on the server, you can click edit and quickly rewrite things in YAML through an embedded VS Code editor, with syntax highlighting and verification that the report still compiles. We don't want full WYSIWYG because we want people to see and touch what is underneath, the Rich Markdown." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text:
Authors customize through declared, validated vocabulary: block YAML, frontmatter and `.rstyle.yaml` keys. No report or style file can inject raw CSS, JavaScript or HTML, and charts accept no engine-level specs or raw SVG; the rewrite proves this with a hostile-input test on every style key and sink (ARC-12, ARC-13, TYP-51). When authors need more, RichView first adds a validated option or a better default. How much a style file may change is decided in part 06 (STY-14).

Later, RichView may allow custom TypeScript components embedded in a report, so authors can build anything they want. That needs its own spec validation and agent skills, and the skills steer agents to use the defined vocabulary and components first and reach for custom code only when nothing defined fits. This is not part of the rewrite.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "Yes. JavaScript and HTML are not allowed, exactly. In the future there can be custom TypeScript embedded components that allow people to do anything they want. For that there will be spec validation, a skill set and so on. So I want to allow any type of code, but there should be skills encouraging the agents to use the defined vocabulary before reaching for custom code." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.
Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "Exactly. That's fairly obvious. Of course there has to be a set of constraints on those." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text:
Rebuild, porting proven modules. The rewrite rebuilds RichView against the accepted lockdown. Existing code and tests are evidence, not a base: a module is ported only when it already meets every accepted item it touches and its tests prove that; otherwise it is rewritten. Nothing survives merely because it exists. Existing tests and fixtures for accepted behaviour become acceptance tests for the new code; tests for rejected behaviour are deleted with it.

RichView is not a production application yet, so nothing needs preservation tests: no test exists only to prove that old behaviour survived. Any feature that is not decided and tracked in the lockdown is dropped, even when today's code has it.
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "Yep. This is true. Given that this is not a production application, I don't want tests that things are preserved because they are preserved. So any features which are not decided right now and not tracked right now will get automatically dropped, even if they are present in current code." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text:
When targets conflict, visual and motion craft wins (INT-12): if a report looks bad, RichView has failed, while a report that is a bit slower or a file that is larger is something RichView survives. People come to RichView for how their analysis looks: perfect text rendering, beautiful charts and images, rich animation. The text carries a report's quality, so storytelling (INT-77) comes right after craft, but the old "80% content, 20% style" framing does not describe why people choose RichView.

Order: visual and motion craft (INT-12); storytelling (INT-77); a short authoring path (INT-13); extensibility (INT-78); low operating cost (INT-15); small footprint (INT-14); speed beyond the budgets (INT-16). Footprint, file size and speed yield to craft; a size or speed budget may be raised when craft needs it, and the change description records the trade.

Guarantees outside the order: RichView is feature-complete for what it accepts and always works; traceability and editability hold (INT-11); safety is never traded (INT-79).
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "I think we go for richer animation. If it looks like shit, we will fail. If it's a bit slower, too large a file or something, it's fine, we will survive that. The 80% / 20% style is the wrong mark, because this is not why people come to us. Of course the quality of the report is based on the text, and text alone can be amazing, as a novel. But we have to have perfect text rendering, beautiful images, all that stuff. We have to be feature-complete. It always has to work." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

Wherever possible RichView makes the performant choice. The language itself does not matter, but Rust is the obvious way to be both stable and very fast, so RichView stays Rust: one shared core runs natively (CLI, server, MCP) and as WebAssembly in browsers and VS Code, and WebAssembly is what makes charts fast in the browser. Handwritten JavaScript exists only where part 03 allows it (ARC-03), and no product rule exists only in JavaScript in the rewrite's target.

The rewrite carries over what Publish strives for, its behaviour and decisions, not its code: Publish's JavaScript is ported to the Rust target when the rewrite reaches Publish (INT-49).

Then: wherever possible we stay with performant choices. I do not care about the language, but Rust makes it the obvious way to be both stable and ultra-fast, so I go for that. And WebAssembly is needed to speed charts up." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text: RichView works first as a single-user tool people download and use themselves, like Microsoft Word: a set of local tools (CLI, MCP, VS Code extension) that create one HTML file, which can be shared and works offline (INT-04). On top of that, like SharePoint on top of Word, RichView's servers (Cowork and Publish) add sharing, roles and approvals (INT-06, INT-83). RichView runs one hosted service, for large data and media (INT-31); everything else works without it.

People will download it and use it themselves, like Microsoft Word, and then it has a SharePoint function on top. For 27 we go with one hosted service for data and media. We have all the functionalities, but it is a set of things you use locally, and you create an HTML which can be shared and works offline. That is what I want to strive for." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

text: RichView Publish is a full member of the RichView family and part of the rewrite. PR #70 is merged into `main` (2026-10-26) and its work continues from there. RichView Publish and RichView Cowork (INT-83) share one RichView server core: an internal component, not a product of its own, that powers both. Publish carries the basic roles and approvals and the live-connector path (INT-06, INT-24); its brief and Git-native loop (INT-22, FEA-BR-26) remain the spec it is rebuilt against (INT-49, INT-52).
note: Dictated by Daniel in the review chat on 2026-10-26: "We have reached RichView Publish; PR 70 is already getting rewritten now, so we merge it in. We have RichView Publish and RichView Cowork, which should share a RichView server core, which is just an internal thing that powers both of those, shared work. So RichView Publish becomes a full, full-scale member of the rest of the family." Recorded by the lockdown agent at his request.

Stories are shared as the self-contained HTML file, as a PDF, and through RichView's servers, which come in two forms: RichView Cowork and RichView Publish (INT-83).
- Anyone can self-host Cowork or Publish.
- RichView also runs hosted Cowork itself, typically at app.richview.ai: people share reports there, including with outside parties. It is free up to limits and paid beyond them; the limits cover how many reports and files an account has and how large they are. Hosted RichView may later have features of its own.
- RichView also sets up and runs a Publish server for a customer under the customer's own DNS records, so it lives on their website.
These paid services are how RichView makes money. Pricing, limits and which features are hosted-only are open.

We are a Cowork server where you can share it, and Cowork also offers sharing with outside parties. We limit how many reports you can have and how big, how many files you can have. In future we could also limit some features if you host on our end, because we have special features just for our website. We host it; typical would be app.richview.ai." Chosen option: Merge into dev, review in the packet.

`dev` evolves on its own against the lockdown's principles, documents and ideas. Feature and design changes merge into `dev` through the gates without asking or pinging Daniel, whether he asked for them or an autonomous loop generated and implemented the idea. Other agents may revert or remove them on `dev`. Gates always run.

Exception: changes to the website or anything highly public-facing do not merge automatically unless Daniel explicitly grants it.

Numbers follow a three-digit rule by default: at most three significant digits, four at most, with a scale word, for example 1.23 million, 167.5 thousand or 167 thousand.

Otherwise what a reader can dig out would differ from what the author and reviewers saw, and could disclose how precise the author's calculations are.

The author can set more or fewer digits, per chart or per element, and can give tooltips a higher precision than labels; readers then see that precision, and no more. There is no warning at publish time.

text:
RichView does not maximize how little an author or agent writes; saving tokens is not a goal. It maximizes trust in the output: the same source renders consistently and to a high standard every time, so an author can rely on it without checking every page.

A chart still needs its type, data, encodings, a title that states its claim, and a source note under it; `richview check` warns when the note is missing (TYP-12, TYP-13, FEA-RP-09). Good defaults and styles carry quality, so agents don't have to tune every chart. They may write as much as they need, and extra source never costs quality. Errors name the line, the problem and the fix. An agent that has read `richview learn` writes a correct first draft without outside examples. Field-level rules belong to part 05.

text:
RichView does five jobs.
- **Write:** the agent turns finished analysis into Rich Markdown with chart-local data, guided by `richview learn` and the skill.
- **Check:** validation and chart diagnostics tell the agent, in machine-readable form, what is broken or unreadable.
- **Present:** one source renders into a typeset, interactive story in any accepted style.
- **Revise:** the human reviews the rendered story beside its source in the editor or browser, and the agent fixes it.
- **Share:** the story leaves as a self-contained file, a PDF or a stable versioned URL.

RichView is not a BI tool: it doesn't run the analysis, and the core never queries data. The one exception is on a RichView server. There, a report can link datasets through the server's connectors (OPN-63), so the server loads the data for it.

text: Readers open a story on a phone, a desktop or as a PDF with nothing to install, and with no account unless its author shared it only with signed-in readers, such as their organization on RichView Cowork (OPN-54, INT-83). Every story reads completely from 320 px wide upward, works with a keyboard, gives charts and controls accessible names, honours reduced motion, and keeps text and tables legible with scripts disabled. Charts render with WebGL (INT-31) and must work in recent Safari, Firefox and Chrome; where JavaScript or WebGL is unavailable, each chart's frame keeps its title, caption and source note and shows a notice that the chart cannot be displayed, with no snapshot, image or table in its place (ARC-05). Readers can reach each chart’s values, at the precision the author chose (FEA-CH-37), and its sources. Every story with an address also unfurls as a rich link preview wherever its link is shared, in WhatsApp, Slack, iMessage, email or a social post: a designed thumbnail of the story, in its own style, with its title, like the card a shared song gets (FEA-SF-55, FEA-RP-51). A story shared only with signed-in readers shows its title and image only to them, so a link preview never reveals a private story. People who meet RichView through shared stories or posts are readers first. The stories come mostly from analysts and also from other writers, such as journalists and people running their own RichView site or blog (INT-06).
